title: The Tannery to the Engine House: Osawatomie Brown and the Blood of the Guilty Land
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Tanner's Son in the Western Reserve

stops.name: Torrington, birth on the road that will take his name
stops.date_confidence: attested. The date is fixed by Brown's own 1857 autobiographical letter to Henry L. Stearns and by the Torrington Historical Society record of the site.
stops.campa: Owen Brown, tanner, and Ruth Mills Brown have a son in the hill country west of the Naugatuck, in a plain frame house on a road that will later carry the family name. Owen is a Calvinist who holds slaveholding to be sin and says so out loud in a state that still has slaves in it. The household runs on scripture, hides, and lye. The boy will describe this beginning himself, fifty-seven years later, in a letter written to entertain a donor's twelve-year-old son. The house burns in a chimney fire in 1918. A granite marker in a clearing stands there now.
suggested_refs: John Brown's autobiographical letter to Henry L. Stearns, 15 July 1857
The John Brown Birthplace Site, John Brown Road, Torrington, Connecticut

stops.name: Hudson, the Western Reserve and the mother's grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for both events: the family's migration to Hudson in 1805 and the death of Ruth Mills Brown in December 1808. The day and month of the move are not recorded, so the date defaults to 1 January to order the segment.
stops.campa: Owen moves the family west into the Western Reserve, Connecticut's land in Ohio, and sets a tannery going among the stumps at Hudson. The boy grows into the frontier: cattle driven, hides scraped, surveyors and Indians passing through the yard, no schooling worth the name. The tannery works straight through the winter of 1808, the winter his mother Ruth dies. He is eight years old. He writes long afterward that he never got over it, that he pined for her for years and could never take his father's second wife for a mother, good woman though she was.
suggested_refs: The Owen Brown homestead and tannery at Hudson, Ohio
sources: Brown's 1857 autobiographical letter to Henry L. Stearns

stops.name: Hudson, marriage to Dianthe Lusk
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1820; the sources in hand do not fix the day, which defaults to 1 January. The birth of John Brown Jr. on 25 July 1821 is attested exactly.
stops.campa: At twenty he marries Dianthe Lusk, daughter of a woman working in his father's household, remembered by those who knew her as plain, devout, and given to warning him against his own pride. They will have seven children in twelve years. He is running a tannery of his own now, separate from Owen's, and keeps a discipline in the house his sons still describe in old age: prayers morning and night, a written account of faults, the rod applied on a schedule. John Brown Jr. is born the following July.
suggested_refs: The account books and household rules of the young John Brown, described in his sons' later recollections

stops.name: Hudson Lodge No. 68, raised a Master Mason
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Master Mason degree, 11 May 1824, on Hudson Lodge No. 68 records as given in the Grand Lodge of British Columbia and Yukon Masonic biography. The lodge record gives no dates for his Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, so the common statement that he took all three degrees within 1824 is inference and is not asserted here. His withdrawal is tied to the Morgan affair of 1826 and is therefore later than this stop.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of May he is raised to the degree of Master Mason in Hudson Lodge No. 68. The lodge is the one body in the settlement that crosses the lines of congregation and trade, and Brown at twenty-four is a joiner of things. He takes to the oaths, the degrees, the passwords, the written articles binding men to one another. Two years later the printer William Morgan disappears in western New York after threatening to publish the order's secrets, and the anti-Masonic fury that follows runs through the Reserve like fire through brush. Brown withdraws and never joins another lodge.
suggested_refs: Records of Hudson Lodge No. 68, Hudson, Ohio
The disappearance of William Morgan, 1826, and the anti-Masonic movement in the Western Reserve

stops.name: New Richmond, the tannery and the post office
stops.date_confidence: attested: the tannery was built in 1825 and worked to 1835, and the postmastership under John Quincy Adams is confirmed by the National Archives. The sheltering of freedom-seekers at the tannery is local tradition and is tagged [R]: no contemporary document names anyone hidden there, and the figure of roughly 2,500 people assisted, repeated on some site pages, is an unsourced round number and is not used.
stops.campa: He crosses into Pennsylvania and builds a tannery in Richmond Township, Crawford County, a few miles from the Ohio line: vats, a bark mill, a house, in time a dozen men working under him. He helps organize a church, opens a school in his own building, and is appointed postmaster under John Quincy Adams. Local memory holds that the tannery hid people escaping slavery in a room off the vat cellar. No number can be got out of any record, and the round figures in circulation have nothing behind them.
suggested_refs: The John Brown Tannery Site, Richmond Township, Crawford County, Pennsylvania, 500 feet south of the junction of PA Route 77 and John Brown Road

stops.name: New Richmond, Dianthe buried with the infant
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1832; the sources in hand do not agree on the day, which defaults to 1 January. That an infant son was born and died shortly before her own death is attested.
stops.campa: Dianthe bears a son who does not live and dies herself within days, at thirty-one, worn through by eleven years of childbearing on cleared ground. Brown buries the two of them together behind the house. He writes about it to his father in the register he keeps for catastrophe: the loss set down, the will of God acknowledged. Of the seven children she gave him, four are living. He is thirty-two, a widower with a tannery running and four small children in the house.
suggested_refs: The Brown family graves behind the New Richmond tannery house

stops.name: New Richmond, marriage to Mary Ann Day
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date. The place is probably New Richmond, Pennsylvania, and is given as such by the sources in hand without full certainty.
stops.campa: Sixteen months a widower, he marries Mary Ann Day, a blacksmith's daughter of about seventeen who has been doing the family's spinning. He is thirty-three. The marriage lasts twenty-six years and produces thirteen more children, most of whom die young. Mary will bury more children than she raises, and will hold the North Elba farm together through the years her husband is in Kansas and in the East. In December 1859 she takes his body back from Virginia in a poplar coffin.
suggested_refs: Mary Ann Day Brown's later testimony and correspondence on the North Elba household

segments.name: The Panic, the Graves, and the Wool

stops.name: Franklin Mills, the land company and the canal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the move to Franklin Mills and the speculation; the day is not recorded and defaults to 1 January. The acreage of roughly 700 and the brief jailing over a seized property come from the National Archives Prologue study and are not further corroborated here.
stops.campa: Back in Ohio he buys into the boom. With Zenas Kent and the Franklin Land Company he takes on something like seven hundred acres along the projected line of the Pennsylvania and Ohio Canal, betting the canal will make the town. He borrows against everything and then borrows against the borrowing. In 1837 the money fails across the whole country, the canal boom folds, and Brown is left holding land nobody will buy against debts nobody will forgive. He is jailed briefly over a property he will not surrender.
suggested_refs: The Franklin Land Company holdings at Franklin Mills, now Kent, Ohio
sources: Paul Finkelman, cited in the same study

stops.name: Hudson, the vow at the Lovejoy meeting
stops.date_confidence: The killing of Elijah P. Lovejoy at Alton, Illinois, on 7 November 1837 is attested. Brown's vow at the Hudson memorial meeting is family tradition, tagged [R]: it rests on recollections set down decades later by his son and others in the family circle, with no contemporaneous transcript and no newspaper account. The month is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: On the seventh of November a proslavery mob at Alton, Illinois, kills the editor Elijah Lovejoy while he defends his fourth printing press. The news reaches the Reserve within the week and a memorial meeting is called in the church at Hudson. Family tradition, written down decades afterward, has Brown standing at the back of the room, raising his right hand, and saying that he consecrates his life from this hour to the destruction of slavery. No transcript is taken and no newspaper carries it. What he said in that church, or whether he stood up at all, is not recoverable.
suggested_refs: The killing of Elijah P. Lovejoy at Alton, Illinois, 7 November 1837
sources: Research dossier, noting the vow rests on later recollection rather than a contemporaneous record

stops.name: Ohio, the bankruptcy in federal court
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date of the federal bankruptcy declaration; the pin is set at Franklin Mills, where the failed ventures were centered, since the sources give only 'Ohio' for the court.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of September the federal court declares him bankrupt. He has now failed at tanning, at land speculation, at cattle droving, at surveying, and at horse breeding, and he has not yet entered the wool trade that will fail next. The record of the declaration names no town, only the state of Ohio. He is forty-two years old, and the whole of what the law lets him keep goes onto a single inventory: household goods, hand tools, and a short list of livestock.
suggested_refs: The 1842 federal bankruptcy inventory of John Brown's remaining property

stops.name: Akron, four children in one season
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1843 from Brown family genealogical and National Park Service records; the month is not fixed and defaults to 1 January. The sources give the location only as the Akron area of Ohio, so the pin is approximate.
stops.campa: In the space of a few weeks dysentery goes through the household and takes four of the children: Sarah, Charles, Peter, Austin. They are buried in a row. He is forty-three and has now buried nine of his own children. The letters he writes that season ask his correspondents about wool prices and about the state of their souls, and do not mention the graves. His daughter Ruth, who survives the sickness, remembers her father standing out at the row of graves afterward, praying that the family be brought to submit.
suggested_refs: Brown family genealogical records of the 1843 dysentery deaths
sources: Research dossier, drawing on Brown family genealogical and NPS records

stops.name: Akron, the partnership with Simon Perkins
stops.date_confidence: attested by 1844 per National Archives Prologue: 'By 1844, he was raising sheep with a wealthy business partner in Akron.' Note that the partnership is sometimes dated 1846 by conflating it with the separate removal of the wool operation to Springfield, Massachusetts, in that year; the two events are kept apart here. Brown occupied the Diagonal Road house from 1844 to 1854.
stops.campa: Colonel Simon Perkins Jr., the richest man in Summit County, offers a partnership: Perkins puts up the flocks and the capital, Brown supplies the husbandry and the management, and they divide what comes. Brown takes charge of the sheep and is good at it. He knows fleece by hand and argues grades with the buyers, and he works out a conviction that the American wool grower is being systematically robbed by the eastern commission merchants. The family moves into the house on Diagonal Road, across from the Perkins stone mansion, and stays ten years.
suggested_refs: The John Brown House, 514 Diagonal Road, Akron, opposite the Perkins Stone Mansion

segments.name: Springfield, Gilead, and the Adirondack Grant

stops.name: Springfield, the wool warehouse on Front Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the move to Springfield, 1846; the day is not recorded and defaults to 1 January. The operation ran there to about 1850.
stops.campa: Perkins and Brown open a warehouse at Springfield, the hinge of the New England wool market. The plan is to take in the western clips, grade them honestly, and hold them off the market until the manufacturers meet the growers' price. Brown grades the wool himself, sorting by hand into bins, and will not come down on a price. The manufacturers decline to be squeezed and buy elsewhere; the growers, unpaid, begin to sue. Inside four years the firm is in litigation from both directions at once. The warehouse runs until about 1850.
suggested_refs: The Perkins & Brown wool warehouse, Springfield, Massachusetts

stops.name: Springfield, Frederick Douglass at the table
stops.date_confidence: attested that Brown and Douglass met at Springfield during Brown's residence there, 1846-1850, and that Brown laid out an Allegheny mountain plan to him. Douglass's Life and Times describes the visit without giving a date; 1847 is the conventional dating and is used here to order the segment.
stops.campa: Frederick Douglass comes to Springfield to look at the white wool merchant the Black congregations of the city keep talking about, and finds a house barer than the houses of the poorest people he knows, a table of beef soup and cabbage, no cloth on it. Brown lays out a plan over the meal: armed bands posted along the Alleghenies, running enslaved people north by the ridge line, drawing off the labor until holding slaves stops paying. Douglass argues against it and goes away unpersuaded, and writes long afterward that his own hope of ending slavery peaceably began to give way from about this time.
stops.quote: but, he added, I will not stay unless you will allow me to pay board.
stops.quote_source: John Brown, on arriving to lodge at Frederick Douglass's house in Rochester, quoted in Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.)
suggested_refs: Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.), on the Springfield visit and the Allegheny plan
sources: Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.)

stops.name: Peterboro, at Gerrit Smith's estate
stops.date_confidence: The Smith land grants to Black New Yorkers and Brown's arrangement to settle among the grantees are attested. The claim that Brown met Smith repeatedly at Peterboro across 1848-1858 is [R]: reasonable and generally accepted, but not documented meeting by meeting. The 1848 date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Gerrit Smith owns something near three-quarters of a million acres of New York State and gives it away by the deed. He has set aside Adirondack land for Black New Yorkers so that they may hold the two hundred and fifty dollars of freehold the state demands before it will let a Black man vote. Brown comes to Peterboro and proposes himself as a neighbor to the settlement: he will buy a farm among the grantees, teach them to work thin cold soil, and stand as one of them. Smith agrees to sell him a farm at a dollar an acre.
suggested_refs: Gerrit Smith's Adirondack land grants to Black New Yorkers, and the property qualification for Black suffrage in New York State

stops.name: North Elba, the farm beside Timbuctoo
stops.date_confidence: attested; the purchase is dated 1848 or 1849 in different accounts and the day is not recorded, so the date defaults to 1 January 1849. The National Park Service gives 244 acres at one dollar an acre. Note that the atlas has carried three different coordinates for this one location; 44.2520, -73.9714 is the John Brown Farm reference point and is used throughout this file.
stops.campa: He buys two hundred and forty-four acres at a dollar an acre in the town of North Elba, under the high peaks, and moves the family into a plank house with the wind coming through the boards. The Black settlement the newspapers call Timbuctoo is scattered across the grant nearby: city men given mountain lots on land that will not carry wheat, in a place where frost comes in August. Brown surveys their boundaries, shares out his crop, and works his own farm badly. Most of the grantees never take up their lots at all.
suggested_refs: The Timbuctoo settlement lands on the Gerrit Smith grant, North Elba, New York
sources: parks.ny.gov, John Brown Farm State Historic Site

stops.name: London, the wool carried across the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: attested that Brown crossed to England to sell warehoused American wool and that the venture failed; the sources in hand give the trip as 1849 or 1850 without a fixed sailing date, so August 1849 is used to order the segment. The loss figure of roughly $40,000 is the reckoning given in Summit County historical material for the wool enterprise as a whole, not for the voyage alone.
stops.campa: He ships the warehoused American clip to England and follows it over, convinced that English buyers will pay what the Yankee manufacturers refuse. They will not either. The English know the wool, find his grading eccentric, and bid under what Boston had offered; some of it is bought cheap in England and shipped back to the same American mills that had turned it down. He comes home to lawsuits from the growers and lawsuits from the buyers. The wool enterprise entire is reckoned afterward at a loss near forty thousand dollars.
suggested_refs: The 1849-1850 English wool-selling voyage and the collapse of Perkins & Brown
sources: Summit County historical material as cited in the research dossier

stops.name: Springfield, the League of Gileadites
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and place. The original manuscript of the 'Words of Advice' was first printed years afterward and survives through Brown's biographers rather than in a contemporary imprint, which the dossier flags and which is recorded here.
stops.campa: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 has made every free Black household in Massachusetts seizable on a slaveholder's affidavit, with no jury and no testimony allowed from the person claimed. Brown gathers men and women of Springfield's Black community and organizes them as the United States League of Gileadites, writing out their instructions himself: go armed, act at once, stand by one another, make no confessions, and if one of you is taken, go to the courthouse. Gideon at the brook sent the fearful home and kept three hundred. Brown's rule of admission is the same one.
suggested_refs: John Brown, 'Words of Advice' to the United States League of Gileadites, Springfield, 15 January 1851
Judges 7, the winnowing of Gideon's army at the spring of Harod
sources: Research dossier on the manuscript's transmission

stops.name: Lawrence, the Wakarusa standoff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. The sons' migration to Kansas Territory earlier in 1855 and Brown's arrival later that year with arms are attested; his part in the Wakarusa War comes from general Kansas Territory historiography rather than a document naming him at a particular hour.
stops.campa: Five of his sons are already in Kansas Territory, farming claims and writing home for weapons. Brown loads a wagon with broadswords, revolvers, and rifles and drives it west. He arrives to find the free-state town of Lawrence ringed by proslavery Missourians and a truce being negotiated over the heads of the men standing in the earthworks. The truce holds, no battle is fought, and the Missourians ride back over the line. Brown tells the men still standing in the earthworks that the leaders who signed it have given away the only argument the other side has ever understood.
suggested_refs: The Wakarusa War, December 1855, and the free-state fortifications at Lawrence

stops.name: Pottawatomie Creek, the broadswords in the dark
stops.date_confidence: attested for the night of 24-25 May 1856 and for the five men killed. Brown's command of the party is not seriously disputed. Which of the men wielded the swords is disputed among sources and Brown never admitted striking a blow; the PBS American Experience account has him firing a final shot into the wounded James Doyle, and other accounts differ on that detail.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of May a proslavery posse sacks Lawrence, throws the printing presses in the river, and burns the Free State Hotel. The next day, in Washington, Preston Brooks beats Senator Charles Sumner unconscious with a cane on the Senate floor. Both reports reach Brown's company on the road. On the night of the twenty-fourth he takes four of his sons and a son-in-law down Pottawatomie Creek, calls five proslavery settlers out of their cabins by name, and has them killed with artillery broadswords ground sharp. He never admits striking a blow; one account has him firing a last shot into the wounded James Doyle, others do not.
suggested_refs: The Pottawatomie massacre site, Franklin County, Kansas, near Lane
The sack of Lawrence, 21 May 1856, and the caning of Charles Sumner, 22 May 1856

stops.name: Black Jack, Pate taken at the ravine
stops.date_confidence: attested. The outcome is firm: after roughly three hours Pate offered a conditional surrender, Brown refused conditions, and Pate and 28 men were taken prisoner. Troop numbers on Brown's side vary between accounts and are not settled; the dossier's own summary tagged this stop [R], which the coordinate and outcome checks upgrade to attested.
stops.campa: Henry Clay Pate, deputy marshal, has taken two of Brown's sons prisoner and is camped near the Santa Fe road at Black Jack. Brown comes on him in the morning with fewer men than Pate has, and the fight runs about three hours at long range through the ravines and the brush. Pate sends out a flag and offers to surrender on conditions. Brown refuses conditions, walks into the camp, and takes Pate and twenty-eight men prisoner. It is the first pitched fight he has commanded. How many men he had with him that morning is given differently in every account.
suggested_refs: The Battle of Black Jack site, Douglas County, Kansas

stops.name: Osawatomie, the town burns and Frederick is shot
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date, the killing of Frederick Brown by the proslavery settler Martin White, and the burning of the town. The size of the attacking force is given variously in the sources.
stops.campa: A large proslavery force rides on Osawatomie at dawn. On the road outside the town they come on Frederick Brown, one of the sons, and the settler Martin White shoots him dead. Brown, a mile off with about thirty men, forms them in the timber along the river and holds the crossing long enough for the town to empty. He is badly outnumbered and the stand fails; he falls back over the water. The newspapers begin calling him Osawatomie Brown, and he answers to it for the rest of his life. He stands on the far bank and watches the town burn.
suggested_refs: John Brown Memorial Park and the Adair cabin, Osawatomie, Kansas

segments.name: Eastern Money and a Government With No Territory

stops.name: Boston, brought in to be looked at
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1857 for the Boston visit and Sanborn's introduction of Brown to George L. Stearns; the day is not recorded and defaults to 1 January. The label 'Secret Six' is retrospective and was not in use at this date.
stops.campa: Franklin Sanborn, twenty-five years old and secretary of the Massachusetts State Kansas Committee, brings the famous frontier captain to Boston to be looked at by men with money. Brown is fifty-six, gaunt, badly dressed, and speaks in the cadence of the Old Testament. He asks for nothing on his own account and everything for Kansas. Theodore Parker hears him. Thomas Wentworth Higginson hears him. Samuel Gridley Howe hears him. Sanborn then walks him over to George Luther Stearns, a manufacturer of lead pipe.
suggested_refs: The Massachusetts State Kansas Committee and the circle later called the Secret Six
sources: exhibits.tufts.edu, 'John Brown and the Secret Six'

stops.name: Medford, dinner at the Stearns house
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1857, days after the Boston meeting; the exact day is not recorded and 15 January is used to place the stop in sequence.
stops.campa: Days after the Boston meeting Stearns brings Brown out to the estate at Medford for dinner. Mary Stearns, who has been reading the Kansas dispatches in the papers, listens to him through the meal and tells her husband afterward that she would sell the house and everything in it to keep such a man in the field. Stearns will end by buying him two hundred Sharps rifles and nearly a thousand pikes. Their son, eleven years old, goes and fetches his savings and puts them into Brown's hand.
suggested_refs: The Stearns estate at Medford, Massachusetts, and the Tufts University Secret Six collection
sources: exhibits.tufts.edu, 'John Brown and the Secret Six'

stops.name: St. Catharines, he calls her General Tubman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by the National Park Service. The coordinate is inherited unchanged from harriet_tubman.journey.json, which carries the same meeting.
stops.campa: He crosses into Canada West in April, a month before the convention at Chatham, to find the woman the refugee town at St. Catharines calls Moses. Harriet Tubman has been running people out of Maryland for the better part of a decade and knows the ground between the Chesapeake and the lakes better than any map of it. Brown wants her routes, her standing among the settled refugees, and her name on the thing. He gets all three. Afterward, and in front of other people, he calls her General Tubman.
stops.quote: Mr. Phillips, I bring you one of the best and bravest persons on this continent--_General_ Tubman, as we call her.
stops.quote_source: John Brown introducing Harriet Tubman to Wendell Phillips, as recounted by Phillips and printed in Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869)
suggested_refs: Salem Chapel British Methodist Episcopal Church, 92 Geneva Street, St. Catharines, Ontario
sources: nps.gov/hafe, 'When John Brown Met Harriet Tubman'
Sarah H. Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869)

stops.name: Chatham, the provisional constitution
stops.date_confidence: attested at month precision only. Wikipedia dates the convention to 10 May 1858 and the research dossier to 8 May; most accounts have it sitting from the 8th to the 10th. The sources in hand disagree on the day, so the day is not asserted and the date defaults to the first of the month.
stops.campa: Delegates gather at Chatham, thirty-four of them Black and twelve white, most of the sessions held in the First Baptist Church on King Street, and sit for three days over a document Brown has been carrying in draft for years. The Provisional Constitution and Ordinances for the People of the United States runs to forty-eight articles: a legislature, a supreme court, a commander in chief, rules for the treatment of prisoners and captured property. One article insists the whole thing dissolves no union but amends one. On the last day they elect Brown commander in chief.
suggested_refs: The First Baptist Church, 135 King Street East, Chatham, Ontario
Provisional Constitution and Ordinances for the People of the United States, National Archives
sources: docsteach.org, 'Provisional Constitution and Ordinances for the People of the United States'

segments.name: The Missouri Raid and the Road to the Ferry

stops.name: Vernon County, eleven taken out of Missouri
stops.date_confidence: attested for the night of 20-21 December 1858, the eleven people freed, and the killing of the slaveholder David Cruise by a member of Brown's force. The identification of the two farms as the Cruise and Larue properties and the finer sequence of the night come from the PBS American Experience account and are tagged [R] in the dossier.
stops.campa: Word reaches Brown's camp that an enslaved family on the Missouri side is to be broken up and sold within days. On the night of the twentieth he splits his men into two parties and crosses the line. They take eleven people out of two farms, along with horses, wagons, and provisions; at the Cruise place the slaveholder David Cruise reaches for a weapon and is shot dead by one of Brown's men. Before daylight both parties are back across the Kansas line with the eleven, the horses, and the wagons.
suggested_refs: The Cruise and Larue farms, Vernon County, Missouri, raided 20-21 December 1858

stops.name: Grinnell, the town that feeds them
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and place: Josiah Grinnell and local ministers housed and resupplied the party at Grinnell, Iowa, on the northward flight.
stops.campa: Eighty-two days on the road in midwinter with eleven people and a child born somewhere along the way, moving mostly at night, sheltering in barns, hunted by marshals in more than one state. At Grinnell the town's founder Josiah Grinnell puts the whole party up, feeds them, and holds public meetings about them in the church while they are still under his roof. Brown keeps the accounts of the flight in the same hand he kept the wool ledgers in, noting down what each town gives: food, money, boots, the loan of a horse.
suggested_refs: Josiah Grinnell's house at Grinnell, Iowa, a documented stop on the 1859 flight

stops.name: Chicago, Pinkerton buys the tickets
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and to Pinkerton's role in raising funds and arranging onward transport toward Detroit.
stops.campa: The party comes into Chicago in a railroad boxcar out of West Liberty. Allan Pinkerton, the detective, at this date an antislavery man with a private agency and a habit of hiding people, raises the money in a single morning from Chicago businessmen and buys the whole party through to Detroit. There is a federal warrant out for Brown and a price posted on him, in a city crawling with men who take money for finding people. He spends the day there and is not taken.
suggested_refs: Allan Pinkerton's Chicago agency and its antislavery work in the 1850s

stops.name: Detroit, thirteen onto the ferry
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and place: more than a thousand miles and eighty-two days from the Missouri farms, the party crossed from Detroit into Canada. The count of thirteen aboard the ferry, including an infant born on the road, is the figure given in the PBS account.
stops.campa: On the twelfth of March, eighty-two days and more than a thousand miles from the Missouri farms, Brown walks thirteen people onto the ferry at the foot of the Detroit river: the eleven taken out in December and two more, one of them a baby born on the way. The Canadian shore is a mile off and the Fugitive Slave Act does not reach across it. He sees them aboard and does not cross with them. The same day he turns east, toward the mountains and the arsenal.
suggested_refs: The Detroit river ferry crossing into Canada West, 12 March 1859
sources: Research dossier on the northward route

stops.name: Kennedy Farm, the man calling himself Isaac Smith
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date, alias, and use of the farm as a staging ground. The distance to Harpers Ferry is about five miles by the National Park Service figure, roughly four in a straight line; older accounts saying seven miles are not followed here. The company at the farm numbered twenty-one men besides Brown.
stops.campa: A man calling himself Isaac Smith, a cattle buyer from New York looking at mining prospects, rents a two-story log farmhouse on the Maryland side about five miles above Harpers Ferry, with a cabin and an orchard. Through the summer twenty-one men arrive in ones and twos and go up into the attic, where they pass the daylight hours in the heat, reading, arguing, drilling in whispers. His daughter Annie, fifteen, and his daughter-in-law Martha, sixteen, keep the place looking like an ordinary household. Two hundred Sharps rifles and near a thousand pikes come in crates.
suggested_refs: The Kennedy Farm, 2406 Chestnut Grove Road, near Dargan, Washington County, Maryland
sources: Research dossier citing NPS Harpers Ferry records

stops.name: Chambersburg, Douglass in the stone quarry
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the day. The meeting is attested only through Douglass's own later recollection in Life and Times, which gives no date; August 1859 is agreed on and the 19th is conventional, used here to order the segment. The 'perfect steel-trap' warning and Shields Green's decision to stay come from the same recollection.
stops.campa: Brown sends for Frederick Douglass and meets him in an abandoned stone quarry outside Chambersburg, sitting among the rocks with fishing tackle as cover. The plan has changed. He no longer means to run people off into the mountains and keep running them: he means to take the federal armory first. Douglass tells him Harpers Ferry sits in a hole with heights on three sides, that Virginia will bottle him up and blow him out, that he is walking into a perfect steel-trap. They argue for the better part of two days. Douglass goes home. Shields Green, born enslaved, says he believes he will go with the old man.
stops.quote: Come with me, Douglass, I will defend you with my life. I want you for a special purpose. When I strike the bees will begin to swarm, and I shall want you to help hive them.
stops.quote_source: John Brown to Frederick Douglass at the Chambersburg quarry, quoted in Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.)
suggested_refs: Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.), chapters IX-X
sources: Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.)

stops.name: Harpers Ferry, the bridges and the armory taken
stops.date_confidence: attested by the National Park Service: Brown led 18 men out of the Kennedy Farm at 8:00 pm on 16 October and held both bridges, the armory, the arsenal, and Hall's Island rifle works by 10:00 pm; three men stayed behind as rear guard. Lewis Washington and John Allstadt were seized shortly after midnight. Accounts saying a force of twenty-one seized the armory conflate the whole company with the party that entered the town.
stops.campa: At eight in the evening on Sunday the sixteenth he tells the men in the farmhouse to get on their arms, and leads eighteen of them down the road in the rain behind a wagon of pikes. Owen Brown, Barclay Coppoc, and Francis Merriam stay behind as rear guard. By ten o'clock the railroad bridge and the Shenandoah bridge are held, the wires are cut, and the armory gate, the arsenal, and the rifle works on Hall's Island are all in his hands. After midnight a detail rides out and brings in Lewis Washington, great-grandnephew of the first president, with John Allstadt and the men the two of them hold enslaved.
suggested_refs: The United States Armory and Arsenal grounds on the Potomac flat at Harpers Ferry

stops.name: Harpers Ferry, the town wakes and closes
stops.date_confidence: attested. Heyward Shepherd, a free Black baggage master, was shot near the station in the early hours and died of the wound. The killing of Mayor Fontaine Beckham, the extrajudicial killing of the captured raider William Thompson, and the mortal wounding of Watson and Oliver Brown all fall on this day; these come from general Harpers Ferry historiography rather than one document.
stops.campa: The first man killed by the raiders is Heyward Shepherd, a free Black baggage master on the railroad, shot near the station in the dark. By morning the militia are in from Charles Town and Shepherdstown, the bridges are retaken, and the raiders are shut inside the armory yard with the whole valley closing on them. Mayor Fontaine Beckham is shot dead in the afternoon, and the crowd takes the captured raider William Thompson out onto the trestle, shoots him, and leaves the body in the shallows. Watson Brown and Oliver Brown are both hit and carried in.
stops.quote: I have possession now of the United States armory, and if the citizens interfere with me, I must only burn the town and have blood.
stops.quote_source: John Brown to the besiegers at Harpers Ferry, 17-18 October 1859; National Park Service, 'John Brown's Raid'
suggested_refs: The Baltimore and Ohio railroad station and trestle at Harpers Ferry
sources: Research dossier, general Harpers Ferry historiography

stops.name: John Brown's Fort, the Marines at seven in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested: United States Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee, with Lieutenant J. E. B. Stuart as aide, stormed the engine house at 7:00 am on 18 October; Lieutenant Israel Green wounded and captured Brown; Jeremiah Anderson and Dauphin Thompson were killed in the assault. The coordinate is the fort's present position, within about 150 feet of the 1859 engine house site.
stops.campa: He pulls the last of them into the armory's small brick fire-engine house with eleven hostages and bars the doors. Through the night he moves between the loopholes knocked in the wall and his two dying sons on the floor. At seven in the morning United States Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee, with Lieutenant J. E. B. Stuart carrying the surrender demand to the door, batter in the panel with a ladder. Lieutenant Israel Green runs Brown through with a light dress sword that bends against bone, then beats him down with the hilt. Jeremiah Anderson and Dauphin Thompson are killed. Brown is taken alive.
stops.quote: I think, my friend, you are guilty of a great wrong against God and humanity,-I say it without wishing to be offensive,-and it would be perfectly right for anyone to interfere with you so far as to free those you wilfully and wickedly hold in bondage.
stops.quote_source: John Brown to Senator James Mason, interviewed on the floor of the paymaster's office at Harpers Ferry hours after his capture, 18 October 1859; famous-trials.com, "John Brown's Interview in the Charlestown Prison"
suggested_refs: The armory fire-engine house, John Brown's Fort, Harpers Ferry National Historical Park
The interview with Senator James Mason at Harpers Ferry, 18 October 1859, hours after the capture
sources: famous-trials.com, "John Brown's Interview in the Charlestown Prison"

stops.name: Charles Town courthouse, indicted and tried
stops.date_confidence: attested per the trial chronology at famous-trials.com: preliminary examination before magistrates 25 October, grand jury indictment and jury selection 26 October, testimony from 27 October, verdict 31 October. The frequent statement that the trial began on 25 October conflates the magistrates' examination with the trial proper. Judge Richard Parker presided; Andrew Hunter and Charles B. Harding prosecuted.
stops.campa: He is carried eight miles to Charles Town and held in the county jail with his wounds unhealed. A grand jury indicts him on the twenty-sixth for treason against the Commonwealth of Virginia, for conspiring with slaves to make insurrection, and for murder in the first degree, and a jury is empaneled the same day. Testimony opens on the twenty-seventh. Brown lies on a cot inside the bar of the court, wrapped in a blanket, rising on one elbow to correct his own counsel. On the thirty-first the jury deliberates briefly and returns guilty on every principal count.
stops.quote: noble old hero whose one right hand has shaken the foundation of the American Union, and whose ghost will haunt the bed-chambers of all the born and unborn slaveholders of Virginia through all their generations, filling them with alarm and consternation.
stops.quote_source: Frederick Douglass, open letter to the Rochester Democrat and American, dated Canada West, 31 October 1859, the day of the verdict; reprinted in Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1892 ed.), ch. IX
suggested_refs: The Jefferson County Courthouse, North George Street, Charles Town, West Virginia
famous-trials.com, 'John Brown Trial Report & Testimony'

stops.name: Charles Town courthouse, the speech before sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and substance. Two transmission lines of the speech text exist and must not be blended: Drew, The John Brown Invasion (1860), p. 82, and the version printed by Sanborn and at famous-trials.com, which ends 'I submit; so let it be done!' The quote given here follows the famous-trials text.
stops.campa: Asked whether he has anything to say why sentence should not be pronounced, he gets up in the crowded courtroom and speaks for a few minutes without notes. He denies any design on the lives of white Virginians and admits without hedging what he did intend. He points out that the book the court makes its witnesses kiss instructs him to remember them that are in bonds as bound with them, and invites the room to consider which interferences on behalf of which people get a man rewarded and which get him hanged. Judge Richard Parker sentences him to hang in public on the second of December.
stops.quote: I believe that to have interfered as I have done, as I have always freely admitted I have done in behalf of His despised poor, is no wrong, but right.
stops.quote_source: John Brown, statement to the court before sentencing, Charles Town, Va., 2 November 1859; famous-trials.com, 'Trial Report & Testimony'
suggested_refs: Drew, The John Brown Invasion (1860), p. 82, for the variant transmission of the speech
F. B. Sanborn, The Life and Letters of John Brown (1885), p. 585

stops.name: Charles Town jail, the letter of the eighth of November
stops.date_confidence: attested. Sanborn prints the letter under the heading 'Charlestown, Jefferson County, Va., Nov. 8, 1859 / Dear Wife and Children, every one' and it is the first he wrote to the family after conviction, six days after sentencing. Citations dating this letter to late November are wrong and the error is common.
stops.campa: Six days after sentence he writes the first letter home since the conviction, addressed to Dear Wife and Children, every one. Through these weeks he is answering letters steadily, to family, to clergymen, to strangers who have written in. In this one he takes the failure of the raid on himself, gives Mary instructions about the North Elba farm and the children's schooling, and then sets out plainly the arithmetic he has arrived at in the cell: that his death will now do more for the thing than his living could.
stops.quote: I can trust God with both the time and the manner of my death, believing, as I now do, that for me at this time to seal my testimony for God and humanity with my blood will do vastly more toward advancing the cause I have earnestly endeavored to promote, than all I have done in my life before.
stops.quote_source: John Brown to his wife and children, Charlestown, Jefferson County, Va., 8 November 1859, in F. B. Sanborn, The Life and Letters of John Brown (1885), pp. 585-86
suggested_refs: The Charles Town jail prison letters, collected in Sanborn's Life and Letters of John Brown (1885)
sources: F. B. Sanborn, The Life and Letters of John Brown (1885), pp. 585-86
famous-trials.com, "John Brown's Letters to His Wife"

stops.name: Charles Town jail, the last visit
stops.date_confidence: attested that Mary Ann Day Brown's final visit took place on 1 December 1859, the day before the execution. The duration of the visit, the supper, and the details of the conversation come from contemporary press reports and family recollection and vary between accounts.
stops.campa: Mary Ann Day Brown is brought up under military escort and allowed in to her husband in the presence of the jailer. They eat supper together. He hands her his will and goes through the disposition of the North Elba property item by item, and asks that the bodies of their sons be got back out of Virginia if it can be managed. The press reports of the visit differ on nearly every detail of it except the refusal that ends it. She asks to stay the night; the escort takes her back out into the dark.
suggested_refs: The Jefferson County jail, Charles Town, and the record of the 1 December 1859 family visit
sources: Research dossier, citing the documented family visit record

stops.name: Charles Town, the note and the gallows field
stops.date_confidence: attested. The final written note handed to a guard is authentic and is printed in Sanborn. Governor Wise ordered roughly 1,500 soldiers to the field and no civilian was permitted within hearing distance; Jackson observed with VMI cadets and Booth was present with the Richmond Grays. The gallows field stood off South Samuel Street; the coordinate is approximate to the block, not to the trap.
stops.campa: On the morning of the second he hands a folded slip of paper to a guard on his way out of the jail. Fifteen hundred soldiers are drawn up around a field south of the town and no civilian is allowed within hearing. Thomas Jonathan Jackson, professor of artillery, stands with cadets of the Virginia Military Institute and writes afterward of the prisoner's unflinching firmness. John Wilkes Booth has borrowed a militia uniform to get inside the cordon, and calls Brown a traitor and terrorizer. Brown waits on the trap with the hood over his head while the troops are dressed into position.
stops.quote: I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood. I had, as I now think vainly, flattered myself that without very much bloodshed it might be done.
stops.quote_source: John Brown, final written note handed to a guard, Charlestown, Va., 2 December 1859; printed in F. B. Sanborn, The Life and Letters of John Brown (1885), p. 518
suggested_refs: The gallows field off South Samuel Street, Charles Town, West Virginia

Victor Hugo's open letter on John Brown, dated Hauteville House, Guernsey, 2 December 1859, appealing against the hanging and printed in the London News in the days following: 'There is something more terrible than Cain slaying Abel: It is Washington slaying Spartacus!'
sources: F. B. Sanborn, The Life and Letters of John Brown (1885)
Wikisource, "Victor Hugo's letter to the London News regarding John Brown"

segments.name: The Body, the Building, and the Legend

stops.name: North Elba, buried by the boulder
stops.date_confidence: attested: buried 8 December 1859 in front of the house, beside the boulder, six days after the execution, the journey north taking about five days. Sources differ on when New York State acquired the farm, 1895 or 1896; the John Brown Farm State Historic Site record gives 1896 and the biography article 1895, and the discrepancy is left open.
stops.campa: The body is released to Mary at Harpers Ferry and carried north by rail and wagon over about five days, through towns where the bells are rung and the shops shut. On the eighth of December he is buried beside the great glacial boulder in front of the North Elba farmhouse, at his own long-stated wish, in ground he never managed to farm properly. The place becomes a destination almost from the week of the funeral. New York State takes the farm over in 1896 and has held it since.
suggested_refs: John Brown Farm State Historic Site, 115 John Brown Road, Lake Placid, New York
sources: parks.ny.gov, John Brown Farm State Historic Site

stops.name: Charles Town, the kiss that did not happen
stops.date_confidence: attested that the story originated in Edward H. House's New-York Daily Tribune account of 5 December 1859 and was established as fabricated by 1885, when the Charles Town jailer's testimony that no such encounter was possible came out during the scrutiny prompted by Hovenden's painting. The 1885 date is used to place the stop at the debunking rather than the invention; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: Three days after the hanging the New-York Daily Tribune prints a correspondent's account in which Brown, on the steps of the jail, stoops and kisses a Black child held up by its mother. Edward H. House, who filed it, was not allowed near the jail; no civilian was. The image is painted at seven by ten feet by Louis Ransom, exhibited by P. T. Barnum in 1863 and pulled that July for fear of the draft riots, lithographed twice by Currier and Ives, and painted again by Thomas Hovenden in 1884. It is Hovenden's version that draws the scrutiny that kills the story. The paintings go on hanging.
suggested_refs: Thomas Hovenden, The Last Moments of John Brown (1884)
Louis Ransom, John Brown on His Way to Execution, and the Currier & Ives lithographs of 1863 and 1870
graphicarts.princeton.edu, "The Legend of John Brown's Last Kiss"
sources: graphicarts.princeton.edu, "The Legend of John Brown's Last Kiss"

stops.name: North Elba, the raiders brought back
stops.date_confidence: attested. Watson Brown died 19 October 1859; his body was taken by Winchester Medical College, prepared as an anatomical specimen and displayed with a label, recovered by an army physician when Federal troops entered Winchester in March 1862, and reburied at North Elba in October 1882 after John Brown Jr. confirmed the identity. On 30 August 1899, the anniversary of Osawatomie, the remains of ten raiders were reburied here in one coffin; parks.ny.gov says only 'several' and one older summary says twelve, and ten is the best-supported figure.
stops.campa: Watson Brown's body does not come home in 1859. Winchester Medical College takes it, prepares it as an anatomical specimen with the arteries dyed and the nerves varnished, and puts it on display under a label naming his father. An army surgeon recovers it when Federal troops enter Winchester in 1862; it is carried to Indiana, identified by John Brown Jr., and buried here in October 1882. On the thirtieth of August 1899, the anniversary of Osawatomie, the remains of ten of the raiders, Oliver Brown among them, are brought to North Elba and laid beside his father in a single coffin given by the town.
suggested_refs: The raiders' graves at the John Brown Farm State Historic Site, North Elba
Winchester Medical College, Boscawen Street, Winchester, Virginia, burned by Union troops in 1862
sources: Wikipedia, 'John Brown Farm State Historic Site'
parks.ny.gov, John Brown Farm State Historic Site

stops.name: Harpers Ferry, the four addresses of the engine house
stops.date_confidence: attested, with one date conflict left open: the John Brown's Fort article carries both 1968 and 1969 for the removal from Storer College, while the Storer College article states the fort stood on campus from 1909 through 1968. 1968 is used here. The pin is the fort's present position in lower Harpers Ferry, about 150 feet from the 1859 site; the date defaults to the year of the Storer move, which is the longest of its residences.
stops.campa: The brick engine house he held for thirty-six hours is sold off by the Baltimore and Ohio in 1891, taken apart, and shipped to Chicago for the World's Columbian Exposition, where the exhibit fails outright. Kate Field raises the money to bring it back; the railroad hauls it home free and it is rebuilt on the Murphy farm two miles from where it began, finished in November 1895. In 1909 it goes onto the campus of Storer College, a Black college founded in the town after the war, and stands there until 1968, when the National Park Service moves it a last time to within a hundred and fifty feet of its own ground.
suggested_refs: John Brown's Fort, Harpers Ferry National Historical Park
The Murphy Farm site and the Storer College campus, Harpers Ferry

stops.name: Harpers Ferry, the two tablets
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1931 dedication of the Heyward Shepherd Memorial by the United Daughters of the Confederacy and the Sons of Confederate Veterans, the attendance figures of roughly 300 white and 100 Black people, the Storer College president's advance warning, the NAACP counter-tablet drafted under W. E. B. Du Bois, its refusal by Storer as too militant, and its installation on the site in 2006. The day of the 1931 dedication is not recorded here and defaults to 1 January.
stops.campa: The United Daughters of the Confederacy and the Sons of Confederate Veterans dedicate a monument to Heyward Shepherd, the free Black railroad man Brown's raiders shot first, inscribed to hold him up as an example of Black fidelity to the slaveholding order. Some three hundred white and a hundred Black people attend a ceremony the president of Storer College has warned in advance may provoke unpleasant racial feeling. The NAACP answers with a tablet drafted under W. E. B. Du Bois, naming the enslaved men and sons of the enslaved who fought alongside Brown. Storer refuses to hang it. It goes up on the site in 2006.
suggested_refs: The Heyward Shepherd Memorial, Potomac Street, Harpers Ferry
The NAACP tablet drafted by W. E. B. Du Bois, installed 2006
Osborne P. Anderson, A Voice from Harper's Ferry (1861), the only account by a Black raider who escaped
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 73843, Osborne P. Anderson, A Voice from Harper's Ferry
